sections.normalized_html: Find a factor of the expression [MATH: 15x^2 - 30x + 45.]
sections.readable_text: Find a factor of the expression [MATH: 15x^2 - 30x + 45.]

sections.normalized_html:
To determine a factor of [MATH: 15x^2 - 30x + 45], we look for a common factor in all three terms.

The coefficients are [MATH: 15], [MATH: -30], and [MATH: 45], which all share a common factor of [MATH: 15.] So, we factor out [MATH: 15] from the expression:

[MATH: 15x^2 - 30x + 45 = 15(x^2 - 2x + 3)]

This means that [MATH: 15] is a factor of the polynomial.

So, the answer is [MATH: 15.]

sections.readable_text: The expression [MATH: 60x^2 + 180x] is equivalent to [MATH: rx(3x + 9),] where [MATH: r] is a constant. What is the value of [MATH: r?]

sections.normalized_html:
We begin with the expression [MATH: 60x^2 + 180x] and compare it to the form [MATH: rx(3x + 9).]

First, we factor [MATH: x] from both terms in the original expression:

[MATH: 60x^{2} + 180x|= x(60x + 180)]

Next, we factor out the greatest common factor from the binomial [MATH: 60x + 180.] The GCF of [MATH: 60] and [MATH: 180] is [MATH: 60]:

[MATH: x(60x + 180)|= x(60)(x + 3); = 60x(x + 3)]

We are told the expression is written as [MATH: rx(3x + 9).] Notice that [MATH: 3x + 9 = 3(x + 3),] so we rewrite the expression as

[MATH: 60x(x + 3)|= (3 ⋅ (60)/(3))x(x + 3); = ((60)/(3)) ⋅ x ⋅ 3(x + 3); = 20x(3x + 9)]

Thus, the value of [MATH: r] is [MATH: \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{20}.]

sections.normalized_html: Factor out the greatest common factor and simplify the expression [MATH: 18x^5 + 27x^3 - 9x^2.]
sections.readable_text: Factor out the greatest common factor and simplify the expression [MATH: 18x^5 + 27x^3 - 9x^2.]

sections.normalized_html:
We want to factor the expression [MATH: 18x^5 + 27x^3 - 9x^2.] To do this, we first identify the greatest common factor (GCF) of all the terms.

Each term shares a numerical factor of [MATH: 9], and each term also contains at least two factors of [MATH: x.] So the GCF of all three terms is [MATH: 9x^2.]

Now, we factor out [MATH: 9x^2] from each term:

[MATH: 18x^{5} + 27x^{3} − 9x^{2}|= 9x^{2}(2x^{3}) + 9x^{2}(3x) − 9x^{2}(1); = 9x^{2}(2x^{3} + 3x − 1)]

So, the expression [MATH: 18x^5 + 27x^3 - 9x^2] is equivalent to [MATH: 9x^2(2x^3 + 3x - 1).]

sections.normalized_html: Factor out the greatest common factor and simplify the expression [MATH: 48 s^{4} r^{2}+60 s^{2} r.]
sections.readable_text: Factor out the greatest common factor and simplify the expression [MATH: 48 s^{4} r^{2}+60 s^{2} r.]

sections.normalized_html:
First, we find the greatest common factor [MATH: (\textrm{GCF})] of the two terms:

[MATH: \textrm{GCF}(48s^4r^2,\ 60s^2r) = 12s^2r]

We now rewrite each term as a product involving the [MATH: \textrm{GCF}]:

[MATH: 48s^{4}r^{2} + 60s^{2}r|=; (12s^{2}r ⋅ 4s^{2}r) + (12s^{2}r ⋅ 5)]

Finally, we factor out the [MATH: \textrm{GCF}] using the distributive property:

[MATH: (12s^{2}r ⋅ 4s^{2}r) + (12s^{2}r ⋅ 5)|=; 12s^{2}r(4s^{2}r + 5)]

Therefore, the expression [MATH: 48 s^{4} r^{2}+60 s^{2} r] is equivalent to [MATH: 12rs^2(4rs^2 + 5).]

We want to factor the expression [MATH: 18x^5 + 27x^3 - 9x^2.] To do this, we first identify the greatest common factor (GCF) of all the terms.

[MATH: 18x^{5} + 27x^{3} − 9x^{2}|= 9x^{2}(2x^{3}) + 9x^{2}(3x) − 9x^{2}(1); = 9x^{2}(2x^{3} + 3x − 1)]

We now rewrite each term as a product involving the [MATH: \textrm{GCF}]:

[MATH: 48s^{4}r^{2} + 60s^{2}r|=; (12s^{2}r ⋅ 4s^{2}r) + (12s^{2}r ⋅ 5)]

Finally, we factor out the [MATH: \textrm{GCF}] using the distributive property:

[MATH: (12s^{2}r ⋅ 4s^{2}r) + (12s^{2}r ⋅ 5)|=; 12s^{2}r(4s^{2}r + 5)]

Therefore, the expression [MATH: 48 s^{4} r^{2}+60 s^{2} r] is equivalent to [MATH: 12rs^2(4rs^2 + 5).]

[MATH: -3(q^5 + q^3) - 4(q^5 + q^3)]

First, we factor out the common binomial:

[MATH: (-3 - 4)(q^5 + q^3) = -7(q^5 + q^3)]

[MATH: -7q^5 - 7q^3]
